title: Revolutionary
reviewNotes: Reconstructed five-piece position after ...Rb1 at 137 seconds. Three checked branches show unique winning Rh8, source seventh-rank skewer with ...Ke6, and explicitly independent drawing/losing attempts. Earlier eight-piece double-rook battle remains source context.
transcript: White is threatening a checkmate in just three moves with the two rooks. So, black cannot allow that and instead he's going to play rook to G6 defending the G7 square and stopping the checkmate. And now both sides have two rooks each and it seems like this position is [music] completely equal. But it isn't because white can start to push this white pawn towards promotion and now be only one square away from getting [music] a new queen. And if black is not careful, white is going to play rook to A8 defending the promotion square. And after something like rook G to G8, white can actually trade one pair of rooks and then play rook to C7 preparing to cut off this rook from the promotion. And if the rook comes to B8, there's going to be a fork like this. Black is going to take and white is going to win. But black is not that naive and he finds a more creative idea to keep the game going and he plays rook to G2 check defended by the pawn forcing the king to move so that after F2, there is a threat of rook to G1. So, both players are threatening to get a new queen and it's a matter of who is going to do it faster that is going to decide the outcome of this game. And to be honest, it seems like black is going to be the faster one because if we promote after rook to G1 check, the king comes out, black promotes and then collects the queen and now this is completely hopeless. But what black failed to realize is that white has the brilliant rook to F7 hanging the rook two different ways. But of course, the rook cannot be taken in either way. If the king takes, white would promote with a discovered check. And if the rook takes, white would promote with a direct check. But most importantly, after rook to G1 check, we would be able to now collect the black pawn and although black can take the rook with check, we would be able to collect this one and now there would be no way to prevent white from getting a new queen. But black is not a fool, he's not going to resign and instead he plays rook to b8, stopping the pawn from in front of it. Now, of course, white can play rook to a8, pin the rook to the king, and now after the king collects our rook, white can collect this one. But now the rook is stopping the pawn from promoting, [music] which gives black the time to give us a check, and then play rook to b1, and sit behind the pawn. And now this position is famously a draw, because whenever the rook moves, this is just going to allow of the pawn. But actually, in this specific scenario, white still has a win with the very smart rook to h8. If black doesn't take the pawn, we're just going to promote with the defense of the rook. But if black does take the pawn, we now have a skewer on h7, attacking the king and the rook behind it. Winning this game.
